# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Clinical Review

## Introduction
Sudden cardiac death (SCD) remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. For decades, the transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (TV-ICD) has served as the cornerstone of primary and secondary prevention. However, TV-ICD systems are associated with long-term complications, notably lead fracture, venous thrombosis, and systemic lead-related endocarditis. The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to eliminate the need for transvenous lead placement, thereby minimizing these intravascular risks [1,2].

## Clinical Evidence and Key Registries
Early clinical experience with the S-ICD was established by prospective registries and cohort trials [3,4]. The international EFFORTLESS registry demonstrated that the S-ICD provides reliable arrhythmia detection and conversion of ventricular tachyarrhythmias in a real-world setting, with low rates of device failure [3,7]. 

The landmark PRAETORIAN trial provided the first head-to-head randomized comparison between the S-ICD and TV-ICD [5]. In this multicenter trial, the S-ICD was found to be non-inferior to the TV-ICD with respect to the composite primary endpoint of inappropriate shocks and device-related complications [5]. While TV-ICD patients experienced more lead-related complications, S-ICD patients had higher rates of inappropriate shocks, though this difference was not statistically significant. More recently, the ATLAS trial corroborated these findings, reporting a significant reduction in lead-related complications with the S-ICD without compromising shock efficacy [8]. Additionally, the UNTOUCHED trial highlighted high shock efficacy and low inappropriate shock rates in primary prevention patients with a low ejection fraction using contemporary programming algorithms [6].

## Patient Selection and Pre-implant Screening
According to current AHA/ACC/HRS [9] and ESC [10] guidelines, the S-ICD is a Class I or IIa recommendation for patients who have an indication for an ICD but lack a concurrent pacing indication (such as bradycardia support, cardiac resynchronization therapy [CRT], or antitachycardia pacing [ATP] for monomorphic ventricular tachycardia) [11]. The S-ICD is particularly favored in young patients, those with limited venous access, or those at high risk of infection, such as patients with end-stage renal disease on dialysis [12].

A unique requirement for S-ICD candidates is pre-implantation electrocardiographic (ECG) screening to ensure the S-ICD sensing vectors can reliably distinguish cardiac depolarization (QRS) from repolarization (T-wave). This screening can be performed manually or using automated software [13,14]. Patients must pass at least one sensing vector in both supine and standing positions to minimize the risk of T-wave oversensing (TWO) and subsequent inappropriate shocks.

## Surgical Technique and Anesthesia
Implantation of the S-ICD involves placing the pulse generator in a subcutaneous pocket over the left serratus anterior muscle, with the lead positioned subcutaneously parallel to the left sternal border. Originally, a three-incision technique was standard, but a simplified two-incision technique has gained widespread adoption [15,16]. The two-incision technique avoids a superior parasternal incision, reducing procedure time and improving cosmetic outcomes without compromising lead positioning. The procedure is typically performed under deep sedation, monitored anesthesia care, or general anesthesia to ensure patient comfort during high-voltage defibrillation threshold testing [30].

## Complications and Device Optimization
Inappropriate shocks and device-related infections represent the primary clinical challenges of S-ICD therapy [17,18]. Historically, TWO was a major driver of inappropriate shocks [18]. To combat this, modern S-ICD platforms utilize the SMART Pass sensing filter, which attenuates lower-frequency signals and has been shown to reduce inappropriate shocks by up to 50% without delaying ventricular fibrillation detection [19].

Excellent shock efficacy and rapid detection algorithms ensure safe termination of malignant ventricular arrhythmias [20,21,24]. Regarding device infections, systematic reviews have shown that while pocket infection rates are comparable between S-ICD and TV-ICD systems, S-ICD infections rarely lead to systemic bacteremia or endocarditis, and management is generally simpler, avoiding the need for high-risk transvenous lead extraction [27,29].

## Future Perspectives
The absence of pacing capability remains the primary limitation of the S-ICD. To address this, modular combinations of the S-ICD and leadless pacemakers (LPs) have been developed [22]. In these systems, the LP provides ATP and bradycardia pacing, while communicating wirelessly with the S-ICD to provide shock therapy if pacing fails to terminate the arrhythmia. As S-ICD technology continues to evolve, these integrated systems, alongside improved batteries and slimmer generators, will broaden the clinical utility of subcutaneous defibrillation [23,25,26,28].
